In [[number theory]], two positive [[integer]]s ''a'' and ''b'' are said to be '''multiplicatively independent'''<ref>{{cite web|last=Bès|first=Alexis|title=A survey of Arithmetical Definability|url=http://130.203.133.150/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.2.2136|access-date=27 June 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121128154616/http://130.203.133.150/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.2.2136|archive-date=28 November 2012}}</ref> if their only common integer power is&nbsp;1. That is, for integers ''n'' and ''m'', <math>a^n=b^m</math> implies <math>n=m=0</math>. Two integers which are not multiplicatively independent are said to be multiplicatively dependent.

As examples, 36 and 216 are multiplicatively dependent since <math>36^3=(6^2)^3=(6^3)^2=216^2</math>, whereas 2 and 3 are multiplicatively independent.

== Properties ==

Being multiplicatively independent admits some other characterizations. ''a'' and ''b'' are multiplicatively independent if and only if <math>\log(a)/\log(b)</math> is irrational. This property holds independently of the base of the [[logarithm]].

Let <math> a = p_1^{\alpha_1}p_2^{\alpha_2} \cdots p_k^{\alpha_k} </math> and <math> b = q_1^{\beta_1}q_2^{\beta_2} \cdots q_l^{\beta_l}  </math> be the [[Fundamental theorem of arithmetic#Canonical representation of a positive integer|canonical representations]] of ''a'' and ''b''. The integers ''a'' and ''b'' are multiplicatively dependent if and only if ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''l'', <math>p_i=q_i</math> and <math>\frac{\alpha_i}{\beta_i}=\frac{\alpha_j}{\beta_j}</math>  for all ''i'' and&nbsp;''j''.

==Applications==
[[Büchi arithmetic]] in base ''a'' and ''b'' define the same sets if and only if ''a'' and ''b'' are multiplicatively dependent.

Let ''a'' and ''b'' be multiplicatively dependent integers, that is, there exists ''n,m>1'' such that <math>a^n=b^m</math>.   The integers ''c''  such that the length of its  expansion in [[radix|base]] ''a'' is at most ''m'' are exactly  the integers such that the length of their expansion in base ''b'' is at most ''n''. It implies that computing the base ''b'' expansion of a number, given its base ''a'' expansion, can be done by transforming consecutive sequences of ''m''  base ''a'' digits into consecutive sequence of ''n'' base ''b'' digits.
